newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: OLYMPICS-OUTSIDERS MAKE DESPERATE LATE BIDS.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-OUTSIDERS MAKE DESPERATE LATE BIDS.

text.p: Rio de Janeiro tried to woo Olympic decision-makers with multiple greetings, Istanbul opted for a tactic of making them feel guilty.
But on the eve of the vote to decide which of the 11 candidates to stage the 2004 Summer Olympics should be on the shortlist of four or five, neither seemed to have done themselves any late favours.

Rio and Istanbul are both considered outsiders in Friday's vote by an Olympic electoral college and their nervousness and apprehension were showing all too visibly as they faced the media after making their official presentations.
The Brazilian delegation should have had plenty of punch as it included the world's greatest ever soccer player in Pele.

But delegation leader, FIFA president Joao Havelange, preferred to keep the ball almost entirely to himself -- and offered up the bizarre thought that the IOC should give Rio the Games because of the number of Christmas cards he sends each year.
"I send 2,000 Christmas cards every year, including to all the IOC members," he said. "And I take the time to add a personal note on each. I doubt if anyone else in the world does that."
Havelange's suggestion that IOC members should recognise this clear sign of friendship when it came to voting for the candidate cities drew a question he did not relish.

The FIFA boss was asked if he also expected an IOC reward for being the man two years ago who organised a petition aimed at keeping IOC president Juan Antonio Samaranch in power after he had passed the mandatory age limit of 75.
"I asked people to sign that petition for the greater good of the Olympics," he snapped back. "They all did it of their own free will."

Pele was left waiting for the pass which never came until the final question of the news conference when he was finally given the opportunity to say how much he thought people in Rio and Brazil would benefit from an Olympics staged for the first time in South America.

The Istanbul delegation appeared to have collectively got out of bed on the wrong side, opening their news conference with an attack on the whole idea of drawing up a shortlist of candidates -- and then blasting the IOC's evaluation report on their bid.
Delegation leader Sinan Erdem said reducing the 11 candidates to four or five without consulting all IOC members was wrong.
"From the very first day I was against this system," he said. "We'll accept the result but the system is wrong. From a wrong system you cannot expect a good result."

The IOC introduced the shortlist to reduce the costs of candidate cities but Erdem said Istanbul had spent 80 per cent of its bid budget anyway and that there would have been little left to do before September's final vote on the winning city.
Yalcin Aksoy, general director of the Istanbul bid, was not content to leave it there, going on to attack the IOC's evaluation commission for errors in its report on Istanbul.
"There were factual mistakes, discrepancies and omissions in the report," he said.
Above all, he said, the commission had failed to recognise the importance of Istanbul's bid as the bridge between Europe and Asia, between East and West.
The only comfort out of all that for Rio and Istanbul was that few observers fancy the chances of Lille, San Juan, St Petersburg or Seville making the shortlist.
Athens, Rome, Cape Town, Stockholm and Buenos Aires are the most likely candidates.
